turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, September 3. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex — and we're starting with the heaviest US-Iran exchange in over a month, because a wedding celebration is now part of this story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: CENTCOM launched fresh strikes on southern Iran overnight Monday into Tuesday, hitting air defense sites, radar, and mine-laying assets — the heaviest exchange since the lull that followed last month's Larak Island strike.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the wedding you mentioned — that's not a euphemism.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No — a strike hit a wedding celebration in the town of Kuhestak, killing at least four and wounding more than 68, many of them women and children. Iran retaliated with ballistic missiles at US-linked targets in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Iraq's Kurdish region.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this stopped being a contained, Hormuz-adjacent skirmish and became a four-country retaliation.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly the shift — every prior round stayed roughly bilateral, oil markets pricing the risk premium and moving on. Missiles landing in four separate countries is Iran demonstrating it won't absorb a civilian-casualty strike quietly, and it puts every US base in the region back on alert footing heading into a week that already had a hawkish Fed and a bond selloff running.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story — Xi Jinping just made a trip he hasn't made in a decade.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His first state visit to Egypt in ten years, meeting President Sisi in Cairo through today, and using it to call for what he's terming a "new Middle East security framework" — landing squarely as Washington's regional standing takes a hit from that same Iran escalation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Beijing picking its moment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Precisely — China's already put over ten billion dollars into Egypt, the New Administrative Capital, a Nile Delta electric rail line, so this isn't a cold outreach, it's Xi cashing in existing investment for a security-framework pitch at the exact moment the US looks least like a stabilizing force in the region.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last world story — Maduro's lawyers just tried something genuinely novel.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores filed papers in Manhattan federal court claiming head-of-state immunity from their drug-trafficking indictment — arguing heads of state are exempt from any national court's criminal process but their own. Judge Hellerstein set oral arguments for November 17th, with trial scheduled for June 1st, 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto business — Uber's finally getting the deal it wanted the second time around.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Delivery Hero's boards endorsed Uber's takeover Tuesday — 41.50 euros a share, roughly 14.8 billion dollars, a 34% premium to the three-month average and well above the 33-euro offer Delivery Hero rejected back in May. Prosus, which holds 17%, has already agreed to tender.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What changed between May and now?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Simply the price — Uber came back roughly 26% higher, and Delivery Hero's own board apparently decided that was the number where continuing to run a standalone European delivery business against Uber's global scale stopped making sense. Shareholder acceptance runs to November 5th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second business story — the UK's having a genuinely busy deal summer.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: UK takeovers passed 100 billion dollars for the year after a Monday surge: Veritas Capital's 1.65 billion pound buyout of industrial heat-treatment firm Bodycote, Epiris's roughly 1 billion pound offer for Gamma Communications, and Norway's DNO buying oil and gas firm Capricorn Energy for about 292 million pounds.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Three very different sectors in one day.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the actual signal — this isn't one industry consolidating, it's private equity and strategic buyers broadly deciding UK-listed mid-caps are cheap relative to global peers, and that's been the quiet story under the London market all year: depressed valuations finally pulling in real capital rather than just headlines about the exchange's decline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto international — the ADP number this morning was softer than the Street wanted.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Private payrolls added just 38,000 in August against a 47,000 forecast, the smallest gain since January. Education and health added 45,000, but manufacturing shed 17,000 and professional and business services lost 16,000 — large firms alone accounted for 34,000 of the total gain.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So small and mid-sized employers are basically flat or shrinking.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read, and it sets up Friday's BLS report after July's negative 23,000 print — two straight soft-to-negative months from the official data feeding directly into whatever the Fed decides this month. And that jobs softness is landing in the same week the ten-year hit 4.814% intraday Tuesday, its highest since November 2023, on a global bond selloff — heavy corporate supply, deficit concerns, and this Iran escalation reviving inflation fears all at once.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A hotter yield curve and a softer labor market in the same 48 hours — that's an awkward combination for one Fed meeting.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's the whole tension in one sentence — markets are now pricing roughly 66% odds of a hike this month, up from 40% a week ago, even as the jobs data argues for caution. Something in that gap resolves loudly either way, and we'll know a lot more by Friday afternoon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets — full board's on the app, and yesterday itself was quiet. Nothing cleared our threshold.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Correct — Wednesday was a stabilization day after Tuesday's real move. S&P, Nasdaq, and Dow all closed modestly higher, Russell up a bit more than the rest, none of it near 1.5%. It's all on the tab; the actual story is what Tuesday did and why Wednesday didn't undo it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Walk me through Tuesday, then, since that's apparently where the real tape was.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tuesday was the Iran-strikes-meet-hawkish-Fed session — oil jumped over 5%, the ten-year hit that 4.814% multi-year high, and gold had its worst day in weeks, down nearly 3%, because rising real yields were beating out any safe-haven bid the Iran news would normally generate.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Gold not catching a bid off an actual war escalation is the tell, isn't it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's exactly the tell — when a geopolitical shock can't move gold because rates are moving harder in the opposite direction, that tells you which risk the market currently thinks is more expensive: a contained regional conflict, or a Fed genuinely willing to hike again into decelerating growth. Right now it's rates, not war, setting the marginal price of risk.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Wednesday's calm — is that actually calm, or just everyone waiting on Friday's jobs report?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Almost certainly the latter. You don't get real conviction moves the day before a payrolls print that could either confirm or completely undercut the ADP miss we just discussed — dealers are flat, positioning's light, and everyone's parked capital waiting for one number. That's not resolution, that's a coiled spring.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what's actually worth watching into Friday?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two things in tandem — whether oil holds this new higher range if the missile exchanges continue, because a sustained Hormuz risk premium feeds straight into the same headline inflation the Fed's trying to read cleanly, and whether Friday's BLS number confirms ADP's softness or reverses it entirely. Get a soft jobs print with oil still elevated and you've got the ugliest possible combination for a September hike decision — slowing growth and rising input costs at the same time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Alex, this one came out of your own inbox this morning, and it's not a markets story at all.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's from the New York Times' evening newsletter — a full investigation into a DHS operation that's been running quietly across all fifty states for weeks now, searching state voter rolls for so-called noncitizen voters.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Quietly how — this is a federal law enforcement operation nobody's been talking about?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Hundreds of DHS agents are involved, and a meaningful number of them were pulled off human-trafficking and terrorism casework to do it. They're cross-checking dates of birth and partial Social Security numbers against DHS citizenship databases, and in some documented cases, agents are effectively logging into individual state election-official websites — sites explicitly marked for individual voter use only — to run those checks one voter at a time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the part that jumps out — agents impersonating individual voters on systems built for the voters themselves.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is precisely the privacy-law question the Times piece raises, and it's happening weeks ahead of the midterms, running alongside a separately contested USPS mail-ballot screening system that several blue states are already calling unconstitutional in court.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the actual scale of the problem this is supposedly solving?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the part that makes the resource allocation genuinely strange — decades of research, across multiple administrations and multiple independent audits, has consistently found noncitizen voting to be vanishingly rare, fractions of a percent in the states that have actually measured it. So you have specialized counter-trafficking and counter-terrorism agents redirected, at real opportunity cost, toward a problem the data says barely exists.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a defensible version of this operation, or is it purely political theater ahead of November?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The administration's public framing is election-integrity assurance — and there's a legitimate government interest in clean voter rolls in the abstract. But the specific mechanism here, agents essentially posing as individual voters on state systems, plus the redeployment of agents from casework with actual, measurable victims, is what turns this from a policy disagreement into the kind of story that invites real legal exposure regardless of the underlying politics.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What happens next — is anyone actually challenging this operationally, not just rhetorically?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Watch the state election officials whose sites are being accessed this way — several are reportedly reviewing whether DHS's access method violates their own terms of use, which could produce an actual legal fight over methodology well before anyone litigates the operation's broader legality. That's the concrete thing to track, not the political noise around it.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy — and the biggest deal in the inbox this morning is a geothermal PPA that's bigger than it sounds.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fervo Energy signed a 396-megawatt, fifteen-year PPA with Google at its Cape Station site in Utah — and Google's holding an option on another 600 megawatts by 2030. Add those together and you're close to a full gigawatt from a single geothermal site, roughly the output of one nuclear reactor.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a serious commitment to a technology that's still relatively new at scale.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: William Blair's analysis puts this single PPA as lifting Fervo's contracted revenue by roughly 65% — that's not a pilot-project number, that's a company's entire financial profile shifting on one contract. And the read matters more than the number: hyperscalers are now underwriting enhanced geothermal specifically for firm, dispatchable load-matching, not as an intermittent-offset hedge the way wind and solar PPAs have traditionally worked.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this confirms the baseload argument you've been making for months.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's about as clean a confirmation as you'll get — Google didn't need geothermal to hit a renewable-percentage target, it needed something that runs whether the sun's out or not, and it was willing to pay up and take an option on triple the initial capacity to lock that in. Watch whether Fervo uses this contracted revenue base to raise its next funding round at a materially better valuation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second item — MISO just filed something with FERC that's going to shape every large-load interconnection going forward.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: MISO filed its large-load reliability framework on August 28th, docket RM26-4 — any load over 50 megawatts now faces four requirements: visibility and reporting, PMU monitoring, ramp-rate limits, and ride-through obligations. Requested effective date is December 4th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does this differ from what PJM's already been doing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: PJM's approach has been queue-specific — fixes targeted at the interconnection process itself. MISO's filing is a blanket operating obligation on both existing and new large loads, data centers and industrial customers alike, which is a meaningfully broader ask. And this is only the first tranche — MISO's full response to FERC's June show-cause order, covering co-located generation and flexible interconnection service, isn't due until November 16th.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this the template other grid operators end up copying?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly the question FERC's own November deadline is going to answer — MISO's framework is now the reference point every other RTO's show-cause response gets measured against, and if SPP, ERCOT, and CAISO converge on the same 50-megawatt threshold, you've effectively got a national standard forming through parallel RTO filings rather than a single federal rule.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one — a transmission study that's really a political argument dressed up as an engineering one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: CERA and S&P Global released a study September 1st valuing thirteen high-priority interregional transmission projects across the Eastern Interconnection at up to 15.3 billion dollars in net system value through 2050 — with PJM alone capturing 6.7 billion of that, versus just 1.9 billion for SPP and MISO South combined.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Who actually commissioned this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: National Grid, the Electricity Customer Alliance, and Converge Strategies — load-serving and large-customer interests, not the RTOs themselves. It lands right as PJM's own board-approved 11.8 billion dollar RTEP baseline transmission plan is already moving, so this reads as building political cover for the next tranche of spending, specifically justified by data-center load growth. Whoever pays for that transmission — ratepayers broadly, or the large loads driving the need — is the fight that's actually coming next.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Dalawang salita ngayon, at pareho itong direktang konektado sa mga balitang Pilipinas na sasabihin natin mamaya.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Una, "kasapatan." Ito ay pangngalan mula sa salitang-ugat na "sapat," at ang ibig sabihin nito ay ang kalagayan ng pagiging sapat o kumpleto na ang isang bagay — hindi na kailangan ng dagdag.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Paano ito ginagamit sa isang pangungusap, halimbawa?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Puwede mong sabihing, "Idineklara ng prosekusyon na may kasapatan na ang ebidensya," ibig sabihin, sa kanilang palagay, kumpleto na ang kanilang katibayan at hindi na kailangan ng karagdagang testigo. Ito ay mas pormal at mas eksakto kaysa sa payak na "sapat na" — ang "kasapatan" ay ang abstract na konsepto mismo, hindi lang ang katangian.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya kung sasabihin kong "sapat na ang pera," pero sasabihin kong "may kasapatan ang pondo," may pagkakaiba ba talaga sa dating?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Meron — mas mabigat at mas propesyonal ang tunog ng "kasapatan," kaya mas madalas itong gamitin sa legal o pormal na konteksto, tulad ng isang paglilitis o isang ulat pinansyal, kaysa sa pang-araw-araw na usapan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang pangalawa naman, "pagbabantay" — mula sa "bantay," na alam nating ibig sabihin ay magbantay o mag-alaga.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama, at ang "pagbabantay" ay ang patuloy, aktibong pagsubaybay sa isang sitwasyon — hindi minsanang tingin lang, kundi paulit-ulit at maingat na pagmamasid, kadalasang may layuning kumilos kaagad kapag kinakailangan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Paano ito naiiba sa "pagmamanman," na natutunan na natin dati?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "pagmamanman" ay may bahid ng lihim o sikreto, tulad ng pagsubaybay nang walang kaalaman ng pinagbabantayan. Ang "pagbabantay" naman ay bukas at kilala — sinasabi mismo ng institusyon na sila ay nagbabantay, walang lihim doon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya kapag sinabi ng isang ahensya na sila ay "nagbabantay" sa merkado, sinasabi nilang bukas at aktibo silang tumitingin, hindi tago?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Eksakto — at iyon mismo ang salitang tama para sa sitwasyon ng BSP ngayong araw, dahil hayagan silang nagdeklara na sila ay nagbabantay, hindi sikreto.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May kasapatan na raw ang ebidensya — sabi mismo ng prosekusyon sa paglilitis kay Duterte, kaya binabawasan na nila ang listahan ng mga testigo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sinabi ni adviser Robert Ace Barbers noong Martes na kumpleto na ang tinatawag nilang "evidentiary puzzle" para sa Article 1, ang bintang na 612.5 milyong piso na kumpidensyal na pondo — kaya aalisin na ang natitirang testigo mula sa AFP, sina Lt. Col. Carlos Sandaan Jr. at retiradong Maj. Gen. Adonis Bajao, dahil sapat na raw ang testimonya nina Col. Boransing at Col. Panopio hinggil sa mga sertipikasyong militar.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English, quickly, for the exact numbers — the prosecution says it's dropping its remaining AFP witnesses because it judges the evidence complete on the 612.5-million-peso confidential-funds charge. The Senate court's also weighing calendar changes to free up time for the 7.2-trillion-peso 2027 budget.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second story — and this one's genuinely large. GCash's parent company, Mynt, filed to raise up to 92.3 billion pesos, roughly 1.5 billion dollars, targeting an October listing. That would make it the largest IPO in Philippine history.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Larger than anything that's listed before — what does that actually change structurally?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's up to 9.23 billion shares at a 10-peso ceiling price, and analysts think it could force the PSE to revisit its 20% public-float rule just to accommodate a listing this size — plus it meaningfully broadens an index that's been thin on tech exposure for years. A fintech this large finally listing is the clearest signal yet that Manila's capital markets can actually host a company of GCash's scale.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third — the peso, and BSP's finally saying something out loud about it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: BSP broke its relative silence, stating it's actively monitoring the FX market and will intervene to address disorderly conditions — but explicitly won't defend a specific rate, because it wants to conserve reserves rather than fight the market head-on. MUFG's now forecasting the peso holding near 62 to the dollar through year-end.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So BSP's drawing a line between watching closely and actually spending reserves to prop up a level.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the distinction, and it's a meaningful one — a central bank that says "we're watching" without committing to a defended rate is telling markets it'll smooth volatility, not fight the trend, which is a much cheaper and more sustainable posture if this dollar strength keeps running on oil and Fed-hike pricing rather than anything Philippine-specific.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last item — growth expectations just got cut.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: OCBC slashed its 2026 Philippine GDP forecast to 3.8%, down from a prior 5.5% call, citing stagflation risk — that would be the weakest pace since the pandemic, down from 4.4% in 2025. No active PAGASA signal today, and the PSEi made no major move, so both stay off the show.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, and both come directly out of the currency story we're about to get into.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First: 不得不 — bùdébù. It means "cannot help but," or "have no choice but to" — you use it when an action is forced by circumstance, not chosen freely.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a more casual way to say the same thing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yes — 只好, zhǐhǎo, is the more 口语, everyday equivalent. 不得不 works in both spoken and written contexts and carries a slightly more formal, almost reluctant weight — it implies the actor genuinely didn't want to do this but circumstances left no alternative. Example: 央行不得不干预市场，以避免汇率过度波动。"The central bank had no choice but to intervene in the market, to avoid excessive exchange-rate volatility."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word — 逆势. I can guess the "逆" part means "against," but walk me through the whole thing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nìshì — literally "against the trend" or "against the momentum." It's a business and finance collocation describing an action that goes directly opposite to where the market or the data is naturally heading.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the opposite version — is there a "with the trend" word too?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There is — 顺势, shùnshì, "along with the trend," which is the far more common, easier move. 逆势 is specifically notable because it's harder and riskier — you're fighting the market's own direction, not riding it. Example: 尽管出口数据强劲，央行仍然逆势压低汇率。"Even though the export data was strong, the central bank still pushed the exchange rate down against the trend."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So today's China story is basically a live example of a central bank choosing 不得不 and going 逆势 at the same time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's precisely it, and it's exactly why we picked this pairing — you're about to hear both ideas in the same three minutes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 尽管出口数据强劲，央行不得不逆势压低汇率。"Even though export data is strong, the central bank has no choice but to push the exchange rate down against the trend" — and that sentence is basically today's whole China story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The yuan has rallied roughly 4% year-to-date, its strongest levels in about three and a half years, riding genuinely strong trade data — August exports beat forecasts, up 9.5% year over year. But the PBOC is actively capping it. Thursday's daily reference rate was set at 6.7807 per dollar against a Reuters model estimate of 6.7167 — a gap of roughly 640 pips, one of the largest downside deviations from market-implied fair value recorded all year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And this isn't a one-off — you're describing a pattern.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Weeks-long pattern — the central bank has repeatedly fixed the midpoint weaker than where algorithmic models say the market actually wants it, which is a quiet, sustained lean against further currency strength rather than any single dramatic intervention.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why would Beijing want to suppress a currency rally that its own trade data just earned?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because a strong yuan and a strong export sector are working against each other right now. Exports are one of the only genuinely strong parts of the Chinese economy — property's still down, retail demand is soft — so Beijing needs the yuan to stay cheap enough to keep that export engine competitive, even though the underlying data would otherwise justify letting it run higher.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So currency strength is actually a policy liability here, not something to celebrate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the real read — it's a quiet admission that this recovery is deeply unbalanced. When growth depends this heavily on exports doing all the work, a reward like currency appreciation becomes something to suppress rather than embrace, because it would undercut the one engine that's actually running. Watch the fixing gap over the next few weeks — if it keeps widening past 600 pips, that tells you Beijing's getting more, not less, worried about losing that export edge.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts — and Berlin's about to host an artist who's never had a major show there before.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Maurizio Cattelan's first major German exhibition, "NIGHT," opens next week at the Neue Nationalgalerie, doubling as this year's Preis der Nationalgalerie. Director Klaus Biesenbach says the new site-specific commission turns Mies van der Rohe's glass box into what he's calling "a church."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a striking way to describe a building famous for being all glass and steel.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's staged alongside career touchstones — "Him" and "La Rivoluzione Siamo Noi" among them — and Cattelan's usual friction runs right through it: innocence staged against violence, memory that refuses to stay buried. Putting that inside Mies's most transparent, most rationalist building is its own kind of provocation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second item — a gallery preview that landed straight in your inbox.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Anat Ebgi's Tribeca space opens two solo shows next Wednesday — Soumya Netrabile's "Field Conditions," quiet, abstracted landscape painting, paired against Alannah Farrell's "Solastalgia," denser, more figurative work in oil, acrylic, and spray, built around grief over a changing environment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two very different approaches to essentially the same unease.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the pairing's logic — Netrabile dissolves that anxiety into abstraction, Farrell keeps it close and legible. Shown together, they read less like two unrelated solo shows and more like two answers to the same question about place and loss.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The Met's new season is opening soon too, and you said the real story's buried a bit deeper in the schedule.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The season opens September 22nd with a new Louisa Proske-directed "Macbeth" — her Met debut, Lise Davidsen and Quinn Kelsey starring, Yannick Nézet-Séguin conducting. But further into the calendar is the actual headline: the world premiere of Missy Mazzoli's "Lincoln in the Bardo," adapted from George Saunders' novel, alongside the Met premiere of Kevin Puts' Pulitzer-winning "Silent Night."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A season built more around new American opera than repertory war-horses.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is a genuine bet for an institution that usually leans on the reliable classics to fund the riskier commissions — putting two contemporary American works this prominently in one season signals real confidence that audiences will follow.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one — Kirkus just revealed its own prize finalists, and the fiction list has a genuinely stacked lineup.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Eighteen finalists across fiction, nonfiction, and young readers' literature, each category winner taking home fifty thousand dollars, chosen out of more than eight thousand eligible titles this year. Fiction includes Tayari Jones' "Kin," Colson Whitehead's "Cool Machine," Julie Orringer's "Luna, Phoenix, Queen," and Douglas Stuart's "John of John."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Stuart again — he's having a genuinely big prize season across multiple lists this year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: He is, and it says something about how deep this particular fiction shortlist runs that a writer with his track record is one name among six rather than the obvious favorite. Winners get announced October 7th, livestreamed, and unlike some prizes that lean toward buzz, Kirkus has built its reputation specifically on breadth of consideration — eight thousand titles read down to eighteen is a real filter, not a popularity contest.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds — and this one's a genuine argument happening inside a single newspaper, not between two different outlets.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Elliott Abrams, the CFR senior fellow who served as Trump's own special envoy to Venezuela, wrote in the Washington Post that the Venezuela oil deal Trump just orchestrated is, in his words, "a shameful sellout." His argument: because major US oil majors wouldn't put up capital, Trump partnered with what Abrams calls "the most shadowy and repellent Venezuelan businessman he could find," effectively legitimizing an unelected, Chavista-linked government — "the great sellout," Abrams writes, "of Venezuela's natural resources and its people's right to self-government."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a serious charge from someone who was actually inside the Venezuela policy himself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which makes the counter-take, published the same day in the same paper, worth hearing in full — a companion piece arguing the opposite failure: that the deal, struck with Maduro's own former vice president just eight months after Maduro's ouster, actually entrenches the same officials and the same policies that wrecked Venezuela's economy in the first place, squandering a reform window a pro-market opposition was genuinely ready to fill.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two op-eds in one paper arguing the deal fails in opposite directions — which one's actually right?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Here's where I'd push on Abrams specifically — he spent years architecting the maximum-pressure sanctions strategy against Maduro, and that approach never produced a democratic transition either, so his "self-government" framing deserves the same scrutiny he's applying to Trump's deal. The arrangement is genuinely ugly, no argument there, but it's also the first one that's actually moving Venezuelan barrels and pulling prices down — and the purist alternative, waiting for a clean democratic partner, has had years to materialize and simply hasn't.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So where does that leave the actual policy debate?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Stuck exactly where it's been for years — every option on Venezuela involves legitimizing somebody unsavory, the only real question is whether you'd rather do that in exchange for oil flowing and prices easing, or hold out for a clean partner that keeps not showing up. Neither op-ed writer has a satisfying answer to that trade-off, and honestly, neither does anyone else right now.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: We're closing today in Glendale, Arizona, with a father and son who turned a four-thousand-dollar repair bill into a nonprofit.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Michael Kuba started fixing his own family's van nearly a decade ago rather than pay that bill, and it grew into The Junkie Garage — a nonprofit that repairs cars for veterans, seniors, single parents, and working families who simply can't afford a shop.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How does it actually work — is there an income requirement, paperwork, anything like that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: None of it. No income check, no paperwork. Customers bring their own parts and pay whatever they can toward labor — an AC repair that could run thousands of dollars anywhere else comes in under 300 there. His seventeen-year-old son Matthew now works alongside him every day.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Thousands of families kept on the road because one guy decided not to pay a repair bill a decade ago.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the whole story, and it needs nothing added to it — that's The Morning Commute for Thursday, September 3rd. We'll see you back here tomorrow.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Have a great day, everyone.
